newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam defence chief in rallying call to military.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam defence chief in rallying call to military.

text.p: Vietnam's Defence Minister, General Doan Khue, issued a rallying call to the country's military on Friday with the publication of a major speech outlining the need for a modernisation and upgrading of the armed forces.

The official Quan Doi Nhan Dan (People's Army) newspaper devoted more than a quarter of its Friday edition to the speech, in which Khue said the next five years would prove a critical period for Vietnam.
Khue, who ranks sixth in the elite politburo, warned that hostile forces were stepping up their efforts to undermine the country's communist government.

He said Hanoi had smashed hundreds of plots to sabotage or incite riots over the past few years and needed to seize the opportunity now to strengthen the military through better equipment, better personnel and increased training.

"We should not allow anyone to trespass even on to a single stone, blade of grass, or underwater coral if that belongs to the homeland," he said, in an apparent reference to land borders and disputed islands and reefs off Vietnam's coast.
"In the current world climate of fierce conflicts between nations and classes, any country that does not know how to use weapons deserves to be treated as a slave," he added.
Vietnam has both land borders and maritime boundaries that are disputed by its neighbours and has clashed with Thailand and China within the past eight years in brief naval spats.
The precise strength of the communist country's military is not known, but according to 1995 estimates it comprises 572,000 personnel with a strategic rear force of three to four million.
Khue said senior officers in the military should pass on their experience to younger soldiers.
He also called for a strengthening of political bonds between the armed forces and ruling Communist Party through a strengthening of the system of party cells.

Khue's speech, originally an address to Hanoi's Capital Regiment, comes less than a week before the 50th anniversary of the date in 1946 that Vietnam formally recognises as the start of the war against French colonial rule.
This year, National Resistance Day on December 19 is being preceded by a high-profile build-up in state media with regular tales of heroism, historic victories and other praise for the armed forces.
It also comes at a time of concern over the health of Vietnam's President, General Le Duc Anh, who is reported to be seriously ill after a stroke he suffered last month.
Anh, 76, is a powerful behind-the-scenes operator in Vietnam's leadership triumvirate of prime minister, party chief and president, and holds sway over the armed forces as a former general.
An official veil of secrecy has been drawn across details of his condition, but diplomats and others say he is not expected to recover sufficiently to resume his duties.
Political observers say Anh's departure could precipitate broader changes in the leadership. General Doan Khue is among several candidates being tipped as potential successors.
